Can you raise your voice to the clouds and cover them with an abundance of water?
Can you send lightning bolts so that they go and say to you, ‘Here we stand’?
Who placed wisdom in the hidden parts, or who gave vision to the mind?
Who counted the clouds in his wisdom, and who set up the pillars of heaven?
Who poured dust over the earth, and who formed the cliffs?
Who gave food to the lion and satisfied the appetite of the lions?
Who multiplied the wild animals in the open country?
And who gives the raven its food? For its young cry out to God and grow faint from lack of food.
Do you know the time when the mountain goats give birth among the cliffs and the deer become pregnant?
Do you keep count of the months, and do you know the time when they give birth,
and when they crouch down and give birth?
And their young grow up and reach maturity.
Who set the wild donkey free and removed the yoke from him?
Who made the open country his home and the salt land his dwelling.
He laughs at the bustle of towns and does not fear the sound of taskmasters.
The mountains in their abundance are his pasture, and he searches for every green thing.
Will the wild ox agree to serve you, or will he spend the night at your manger?
Can you fasten a yoke on the wild ox’s neck, and will he pull a plow over difficult ground?
Do you trust him because his strength is great, and leave your labor to him?
Do you trust him to clear your threshing floor and gather your grain?
She proudly displays her splendid wings; she flies, returns, and nests.
She leaves her eggs on the ground and warms them on the dust.
She forgets that she has a bird’s feet and that a wild animal tramples her.
She has produced many young that are not hers, and she has labored in vain, without fear.
For God has made wisdom abundant, but has not given her a share of understanding.
She rises high like a palm tree and laughs at the horse and its rider.
Do you give the horse his strength and clothe his neck with armor?
Do you make him leap like a locust, or frighten him with terror?
He paws deeply and rejoices in the valley, and goes out armed to meet the enemy.
He laughs at the pit and is not afraid; he does not turn back before the sword.
Above him the quiver flaunts itself, along with the flashing spear and javelin.
With excitement and fury he races over the ground and does not fear the sound of the horn.
At its sound he says, “Aha!” From far away he smells battle and startles the commanders with his neighing.
Does the hawk come into being through your wisdom and spread his wings toward the south?
Does the eagle rise at the command of your mouth and place his nest high on a cliff?
He dwells and spends the night on the pointed crag.
He feeds on his prey, and his eyes gaze into the distance.
His young gulp down blood, and wherever someone lies slain, there he is.
Then the Lord answered and said to Job:
God’s counsels are many, and whoever reproves God must give an answer.
Job answered and said to the Lord:
“I am insignificant. What can I answer you? I have put my hand over my mouth.
I have spoken once, and I will not answer; twice, and I will say no more.”
The Lord answered Job from the whirlwind and said:
“Now brace yourself like a warrior. I will question you, and you must tell me.
Will you overrule me and condemn me so that you may be in the right?
Do you have an arm like God’s, and can you thunder with a voice like his?
Clothe yourself in majesty and strength, and wrap yourself in splendor and glory.
Pour out your furious anger; look at everyone who is exalted and bring him down.
Throw down the wicked where they stand.
Bury them together in the dust, and bind their faces in the ashes.
Then I too will praise you, when your own right hand has saved you.
Look at Behemoth, which I made along with you; it eats grass like an ox.
And his strength is in his back.
He raises his tail like a cedar, and the sinews of his thighs are taut.
Its bones are strong like bronze and like iron.
He is the foremost of all God’s creatures; God made him to wage war.
The mountains bring him abundance, and so do all the wild animals.
He sleeps beneath its shade and lies down in the shelter of the reeds.
Shadows surround him, and the willows of the stream surround him.
If the river surges, he does not tremble; he is confident that the Jordan will pour into his mouth.
They seize him by his [?], and he will be caught in a trap.
Can you catch the sea monster in a trap? Can you catch him by his tongue with a rope?
Can you put a bridle in his mouth and pierce his jaw with a [?]?
Will he plead earnestly with you and speak gentle words to you?
Will he make a covenant with you, or will you take him as a servant forever?
Will you play with him like a bird and keep him for the days of your youth?
Will partners gather over him and divide him among many?
Will you fill his skin with flesh and his head with the shadow of fire?
Lay your hand on him; remember the battle, and do not do it again.
Look, your foot is loose, and even God will take away his gall.
He will not retreat when he is roused; and who can stand before me?
Who has given to me first, so that I should repay him? Everything under heaven is mine.
I will not be silent about his strength and the sinews of his might.
Who has uncovered the surface of his clothing? And when the net falls, who comes?
Who opens the door of his mouth? Around his teeth is terror.
For in the ravine his mouth is bound, tied, and sealed.
They are close to one another, and no air enters between them.
They cling to one another, holding fast and not coming apart.
His appearances are full of light, and his eyes are like the rays of dawn.
Torches come out of his mouth like fiery coals, blazing like sparks of fire.
Smoke comes out of his nostrils like the fire of a pot being heated.
His breath sets coals ablaze, and flames come out of his mouth.
Strength lodges in his neck, and terror leaps before him.
His flesh is splendid and fat, firmly supported and unmoving.
His heart is cast like stone and made firm like flint.
The mighty tremble in fear of him, and those who stand firm are brought low.
The gate of the companion who cannot stand [?]; he takes up the spears of the mighty.
He considers iron like straw, and bronze like wood struck by an axe.
He does not flee from the bow, and he considers slingstones like stalks.
He laughs at the javelin.
He considers the deep like dry land.
And his strength walks upon the dust; he was made for destruction.
He saw everything that was lofty, and he became king over all creeping creatures.
Then Job answered and said to the Lord:
“I know that you have the power to do all these things, and no thought is hidden from you.
Who is this who devises counsel with words without knowledge? Therefore you showed me things I did not understand or know, things too great for me.
Listen to me, and I will speak. I will ask you, and you teach me.
I had heard of you only by hearing with my ears, but now my eye has seen you.
Therefore I will be silent and repent in dust and ashes.”

After the Lord had spoken these words to Job, the Lord said to Eliphaz the Temanite, “My anger has burned against you and your two friends, because you have not spoken rightly before me as my servant Job has.

Now take seven bulls and seven rams, and go to my servant Job. Let him offer a sacrifice on your behalf, and let my servant Job pray for you. I will show him favor, so that I do not bring you into disgrace, because you have not spoken rightly before me as my servant Job has.”
So Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite went and did as the Lord had told them, and the Lord showed favor to Job.
The Lord restored Job’s fortunes as he prayed for his friends, and the Lord gave Job twice as much as he had possessed.

All his brothers and sisters and everyone who had known him before came to him and ate bread with him in his house. They had grieved over him, and they comforted him for all the calamities the Lord had brought upon him. Each gave him a ewe and a gold earring.
The Lord blessed Job’s later life more than his earlier life. He had fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, a thousand pairs of oxen, and a thousand female donkeys.
He also had seven sons and three daughters.
He named the first Jemimah, the second Keziah, and the third Keren-happuch.
In all the land no women were found as beautiful as Job’s daughters, and their father gave them an inheritance along with their brothers.
After this Job lived a hundred and forty years, and he saw his children and his children’s children for four generations.
Job grew old and was full of days, and he died.
